Adult specimens of Kampen, Ilisha kampeni, reach a maximum standard length of 16 cm [Li = 16 cm], though individuals in less productive coastal habitats seldom exceed 14 cm. In the warm, stable waters typical of their tropical distribution, maintained experimentally at 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C], the yolk-sac larvae complete the transition to exogenous feeding by approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days] after hatching. This rapid onset of active feeding is characteristic of clupeiform larvae that inhabit productive nearshore environments, where early prey availability is high. Following this period of lecithotrophic absorption, the developing fish enter a pelagic larval phase during which somatic growth proceeds quickly. Field surveys suggest that juveniles disperse widely along the continental shelf, taking advantage of plankton-rich surface layers. The species exhibits a relatively compressed early life history, consistent with other small-bodied clupeiforms that prioritize rapid early growth to reduce vulnerability to size-selective predation during the vulnerable postflexion stage.

Sexual maturation in Ilisha kampeni begins once individuals reach a standard length of approximately 10 cm [Lp = approximately 10 cm], a threshold commonly reported for clupeids inhabiting the Indo-Pacific region. At this size, corresponding to a wet body mass of around 17.5 grams [Wwp = around 17.5 grams], vitellogenesis becomes histologically detectable in females and the onset of gametogenesis occurs in males. The body mass at the onset of reproductive activity is relatively modest, reflecting a life-history strategy in which reproductive investment begins early relative to ultimate size. The species shows a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 3.8% [GSI = 3.8%] when maintained under laboratory conditions at 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C]. This value indicates a moderate allocation of somatic tissue toward ovarian mass during the spawning season, consistent with iteroparous clupeids that produce multiple batches of eggs over an extended breeding period. The gonadal recrudescence pattern suggests that reproductive activity is tightly coupled with thermal conditions, with peak spawning coinciding with the warmest months of the year across its range.

The maximum attainable wet body mass in Kampen, based on the length-weight relationship derived from extensive sampling, is approximately 72.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 72.9 grams], though this asymptotic value is rarely observed in wild-caught specimens due to high natural mortality rates. In contrast, dry mass at the moment of eclosion is extremely low, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.0038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0038 grams]. This very small initial mass reflects the minute egg diameter of roughly 1.94 mm, a feature common among pelagic-spawning clupeiforms that produce large numbers of small, transparent eggs. The substantial increase from birth to adult mass, a factor of nearly 20,000, implies a rapid growth trajectory during the early juvenile phase. Comparing the observed birth mass to that of related taxa suggests that Ilisha kampeni invests in high fecundity rather than large offspring size, a strategy well suited to the variable productivity of tropical coastal ecosystems where larval survival is unpredictable.

Under constant thermal conditions of 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C], the maximum documented lifespan for Ilisha kampeni in the wild is approximately 365 days [am = approximately 365 days], or one full annual cycle. This short lifespan classifies the species as an obligate annual, completing its entire life history within a single year. Such a compressed schedule is typical of many small, fast-growing clupeids that inhabit warm, seasonally productive waters. The roughly 365-day maximum lifespan (roughly 365 days) [am = roughly 365 days] is consistent with the rapid maturation and early reproduction described above, as individuals must breed before the onset of senescence-related mortality at a temperature of 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C]. In contrast to longer-lived clupeiforms such as certain Alosa species, which may persist for several years, the annual life cycle of Ilisha kampeni appears to be an adaptation to the strong seasonal pulses of productivity that characterise its coastal habitat. Field recapture data suggest that few individuals survive beyond the post-spawning period, with most mortality concentrated in the weeks immediately following reproduction.

The standard length at puberty for female Kampen has been estimated at approximately 10 cm [Lp = approximately 10 cm], corroborating field observations that the smallest gravid individuals captured in trawl surveys consistently exceed this size threshold. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 17.5 grams [Wwp = 17.5 grams] represents roughly one-quarter of the ultimate wet weight of approximately 72.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 72.9 grams], indicating that reproductive activity commences well before asymptotic size is approached. The gonadosomatic index reached a peak of 3.8% [GSI = 3.8%] at 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C]. This sustained reproductive investment is energetically demanding, yet it allows the species to capitalise on the extended warm season typical of tropical latitudes. Together, these life-history traits portray Ilisha kampeni as a fast-growing, early-maturing, annual clupeid that optimises reproductive output within a narrow temporal window.
